archetype.name: Dual-Threat (veteran backup)
archetype.definition: A 12-year veteran QB2 who has always paired a functional, mostly timing-based passing game with real running ability, now used as Washington's insurance behind Jayden Daniels.

report.headline: Efficient, turnover-free relief work, but a 51-attempt sample flatters him
report.take:
Marcus Mariota is Washington's backup, and his 2026 line is relief duty. He came on for 45% of the snaps at Dallas in Week 2, played the full game against Seattle in Week 3, and got the Week 4 start against Indianapolis but was on the field for only 16% of snaps. Daniels has started every game since. That leaves 51 attempts, which is enough to describe how he played but not enough to measure him. His 0.21 EPA per dropback ranks 9th of 49 qualifiers, and his 3.89 CPOE ranks 11th. That reads like a starter's efficiency, and it mostly holds up against what he has always been: a mobile, accurate-enough passer who doesn't hand away possessions.

The engine is the short game. On throws under 10 air yards he completed 77.8% with a 7.5 CPOE, and the 0-9 bucket alone produced 11.7 EPA, more than all his passing combined. Throws to the left (15.1 CPOE) and Terry McLaurin (0.419 EPA per target) carried the rest. He was less aggressive than last year, with aggressiveness down 4.9 points, and that conservatism is part of why he threw zero interceptions after giving away 0.78 a game in 2025. The legs showed up too. Two designed runs went for 22 yards a carry, which fits a career where his rushing yards ranked inside the top 10 in most seasons.

The numbers hide some problems. His 7.8% TD rate ranks 3rd, on top of 4 touchdowns that came on a handful of red-zone and deep throws; half of those TDs came on deep passes he completed only 25% of the time. His best football came in catch-up mode, with 0.604 EPA per play while trailing by 9+ against -0.014 within one score. Third down was poor: a 26.7% conversion rate on 7.4 yards to go. He was also pressured on 38.9% of dropbacks, the highest rate among 42 charted passers, so he was under siege when he played. His 14.3% pressure-to-sack rate ranks 1st, a sharp break from career rates between 31% and 42%, and on this few dropbacks that looks more like luck than a new skill.

Going forward, Mariota's value is as an option rather than a producer. If Daniels stays healthy, he throws few or no passes. If he's pressed into starts, expect a competent, low-turnover game manager whose efficiency drifts down toward his career norm (EPA per play between 0.035 and 0.125 across his seasons) as the TD rate and sack avoidance cool.

strengths.title: Accurate, efficient short passing
strengths.body: Under 10 air yards he completed 77.8% of throws, well over expected, and the short bucket supplied the bulk of his EPA. The ball came out on time to McLaurin and to the left side, and his CPOE has sat above +3 in two of his last three seasons, so the accuracy is real. The level of efficiency will fade with volume, but the profile holds.

strengths.title: Zero giveaways
strengths.body: He has no interceptions and no lost fumbles, both ranking 1st. That follows a 2025 in which he threw 0.78 picks a game. Lower aggressiveness is part of the cause and is a sustainable choice. A spotless line over 51 attempts isn't sustainable; his career has typically carried 7-15 interceptions a season.

strengths.title: Legs still a real weapon
strengths.body: His two designed runs went for 22 yards a carry, and he rushed for 35 yards in his brief Week 4 start. Rushing has been a top-10 trait in most of his seasons, so it gives a backup a floor most QB2s lack.

concerns.title: TD rate and sack avoidance will regress
concerns.body: A 7.8% TD rate ranks 3rd, and 2 of the 4 TDs came on deep balls he completed at only a 25% clip. His 14.3% pressure-to-sack rate ranks best in the league, but it contradicts his entire career, so expect both to fall back. Neither reflects a skill change backed by a cause.

concerns.title: Production skewed to catch-up script
concerns.body: He was excellent while trailing by 9 or more and roughly average within one score. Third down was where drives died: 26.7% conversions with 2 sacks. Some of the shine came against Dallas's 31st-ranked defense in a lopsided loss.

concerns.title: Heavy pressure behind this line
concerns.body: He faced pressure on 38.9% of dropbacks, worst among charted passers. Washington's offense ranks 23rd in hit rate allowed, so the cause is mostly the protection rather than him. A concussed guard in Lucas Patrick doesn't help if Mariota has to play.

trend.note: He went from 45% of snaps in Week 2 to a full game in Week 3 and then just 16% in his Week 4 start. He hasn't factored since Daniels resumed starting in Week 5.

nextGame.headline: Only relevant if Daniels goes down; Giants limit deep shots
nextGame.body:
The Giants are a mixed matchup for his style. They're stingy deep, ranking 3rd in deep EPA allowed and 7th in explosive pass rate, and that takes away the shots that produced half his TDs. They don't hit the quarterback much, ranking 28th in hit rate, which would ease his biggest problem. And though they rank 3rd in passing yards allowed to QBs, they rank 27th in TDs allowed. Offenses run more against them than usual, making them a strong run funnel that suits Washington's ground game more than a backup's arm. It's a short week on four days' rest, with light drizzle in the forecast.

Availability is the whole story for him. Daniels isn't on the injury report, so Mariota projects as a clipboard holder. If he's needed, his receiving group is thin: Treylon Burks is out, Dyami Brown is on IR, and Chig Okonkwo is questionable with a hip injury. That makes McLaurin and Rachaad White even more central. On the other side, Abdul Carter (87% of snaps) is questionable, and his absence would further soften an already light Giants pressure profile.

keyMatchups.title: Giants' deep coverage versus his shots
keyMatchups.body: New York allows strongly negative EPA on deep throws, and Mariota completed only a quarter of his deep attempts this year. Any relief appearance will run through the short game.

keyMatchups.title: Light Giants pass rush
keyMatchups.body: The Giants rank 28th in hit rate, a relief for a QB who faced the league's highest pressure rate. Carter's status could tilt that further.

keyMatchups.title: McLaurin as the safety valve
keyMatchups.body: With Burks out and Brown on IR, McLaurin is the target who produced for Mariota. Opposing WR1s have scored slightly over their averages against this defense, though they managed only modest EPA per target.

nextGame.watch: Whether Daniels takes every snap; Mariota only gets snaps if Daniels gets hurt or the game turns into a blowout.

restOfSeason.body: As QB2, his expected weekly output is close to zero, with the upside tied entirely to Daniels' health. If he does start, the role-driven parts should hold: short-area accuracy, rushing value and low turnovers. The 7.8% TD rate, the clean interception line and the league-best sack avoidance under pressure won't. A realistic starting line looks like his 2025 version, which averaged 188.3 passing yards a game with about one TD, a pick most weeks and roughly 30 rushing yards, behind a line that lets pressure through.

confidence.note: 51 attempts, mostly in relief, and he's currently the backup with no snaps since Week 4.
